paragraphs.heading: A rock that splits
paragraphs.text: Schist is a medium-grained metamorphic rock, generally derived from a fine-grained sedimentary rock such as shale. Its mark is strong schistosity. That means its mineral grains, which are easy to see with a low-power hand lens, are lined up so that the rock splits easily into thin flakes or plates. The name goes back to the Greek word schízein, "to split".

paragraphs.heading: What it is made of
paragraphs.text: The texture reflects a large share of platy minerals. Mica, chlorite, talc and graphite are examples. Minerals of a more granular kind, such as quartz or feldspar, often lie between them. The grains are typically 0.25 to 2 millimeters across, and typically more than half of them share a preferred orientation. Schists also very often hold porphyroblasts, single crystals of unusual size, of minerals such as garnet.

paragraphs.heading: How the layering forms
paragraphs.text: Schistosity develops at raised temperature when a rock is squeezed harder in one direction than in the others. That kind of stress is typical of regional metamorphism in places where mountains are being built. Platy minerals are turned or recrystallised into parallel layers. The schistosity forms at right angles to the direction of greatest compression.

paragraphs.heading: From mud to schist
paragraphs.text: Mudstone shows the steps. Early metamorphism turns it into slate, a very fine-grained metamorphic rock, and more metamorphism turns the slate into fine-grained phyllite. Further recrystallization gives medium-grained mica schist, in which the clay minerals of the mudstone have become mica. If metamorphism goes on, dehydration reactions change platy minerals into granular ones such as feldspars. Schistosity then drops and the rock becomes a gneiss.

paragraphs.heading: Many starting rocks
paragraphs.text: Schists are defined by their texture, not by what they are made of, and their mineral makeup can vary greatly. They can form from many kinds of rock, among them mudstones, which are sedimentary, and tuffs, which are igneous. Chlorite schist and talc schist typically form by metamorphism of ultramafic igneous rocks. Graphite schist is uncommon, but it can form from sedimentary beds that held plenty of organic carbon.

paragraphs.heading: Names and building sites
paragraphs.text: The original rock is called the protolith. Where its type can still be made out, the schist usually gets a name that reflects it, such as schistose metasandstone. Otherwise the minerals go into the name, as in quartz-feldspar-biotite schist, a schist of uncertain protolith that holds quartz, feldspar and biotite mica. For civil engineers, schist bedrock can be a challenge, because it has pronounced planes of weakness.
